blurb: Join a 7-person AI startup in San Francisco, or take the stable role in Seattle?

decision.title: Startup SF vs Stable Seattle
decision.question: Should I join the 7-person AI startup in San Francisco or take the stable software engineering role in Seattle?

A.label: AI startup in SF
A.summary: In this simulated world, you learn fast and own product areas from the start on a 7-person team. In this world, the startup misses its raise, closes around month 19, and you rebuild into senior product scope by year five.
top_tradeoffs: More fast broad learning, less deep specialization
More early ownership, less job security
More SF AI network, less savings and rest

persona.voice: "I learned fast and owned real work. I also learned how fast a buffer can go."

comparison.summary: Against your stated priorities, learning 5/5 and ownership 5/5 fit path A better in the early years, while stability 4/5 fits path B better across all years. In this simulated comparison, A buys speed and scope with more risk to your $40K starting buffer, while B buys calm, savings, and time with slower growth in breadth. Location at 3/5 does not decide it here, since your current city and local ties are unknown.
dominant_assumptions: In this world, the SF startup closes around month 19 and its unspecified equity ends at zero.
In this world, SF housing stays in the $41K-$48K per year range unless shared, while Seattle housing stays in the $23K-$27K per year range.
In this world, Seattle pay stays cash only with slow raises, and scope grows only with tenure.

Proof that the Seattle team offers AI work, real scope, or a faster promotion path.
A clear SF housing plan, shared or solo, that keeps monthly spend near your stated $4,500 baseline.

front_pages.deck: In this simulated world, equity fell to $0 after a month-17 rehire. Work settled to 40-45 hour weeks while savings rebuilt from $59K to $86K.
front_pages.changed_because: Startup shutdown at month 14 forced a job search and month-17 rehire, which reset the role to new hire and cut equity to $0.

front_pages.headline: Promoted in Seattle as Steady Work Continued
front_pages.deck: In this simulated world, senior role and 40-hour weeks held steady. Savings grew to $182K to $202K with regular routines.
front_pages.changed_because: Shock did not reach this branch because the Seattle role is at an established company, not the failed AI startup.

verdict.why: In this simulated world, B kept pay and savings while A lost equity and faced a pay gap. B had no job search or rehire.
verdict.dominant_assumption: Seattle employer stays funded and employed through year 2.

comparison.summary: Against your stated priorities, learning 5/5 and ownership 5/5 fit path A better in the early years, while stability 4/5 fits path B better across all years. In this simulated comparison, A buys speed and scope with more risk to your $40K starting buffer, while B buys calm, savings, and time with slower growth in breadth. Location at 3/5 does not decide it here, since your current city and local ties are unknown.
dominant_assumptions: In this world, the SF startup closes around month 19 and its unspecified equity ends at zero.
In this world, SF housing stays in the $41K-$48K per year range unless shared, while Seattle housing stays in the $23K-$27K per year range.
In this world, Seattle pay stays cash only with slow raises, and scope grows only with tenure.
what_would_change_my_mind: Clear facts on startup runway, cash, and equity terms. Unknown equity is a major gap.
Proof that the Seattle team offers AI work, real scope, or a faster promotion path.
A clear SF housing plan, shared or solo, that keeps monthly spend near your stated $4,500 baseline.

messages.text: I regret those late nights for launch [E-A-006] and the sustained high stress around shipping [ev_A_012]. My hardest part was the startup closing after a failed raise [E-A-003], when my job ended and equity was worth zero [ev_A_018].

I hear you on the late nights, that is not my life here. I kept stable 40-hour weeks with manageable on-call pressure [ev_U_006] [ev_B_009]. What I regret is ownership limited to small features and solid skills with less breadth [ev_U_011] [ev_B_020].

I don't miss easy weeks — I lived 50-55 hour weeks as core contributor [ev_U_003] with sustained high stress around shipping [ev_A_012]. I regret that our startup closed after a failed raise [E-A-003] and my equity ended worth zero [ev_A_018]. Unlike you, I got solid options from breadth and story [ev_A_008] but stayed a strong generalist with thinner deep specialization [ev_A_008].
